narrative:
The model predicted a 72.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure. These two performance measures outweighed everything else. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential feature, but it worked in the opposite direction, modestly increasing the chance you would pass.

In practical terms, your first-year and third-year rankings placed you at the very bottom of your school’s distribution—far below the average student who was admitted. Your LSAT score of 31 was also noticeably lower than the 37-point average of accepted applicants. While your undergraduate GPA of 3.20 is almost identical to the typical admitted student and your upper-middle family income is actually the most common background among those accepted, these positives could not overcome the clear academic ranking signals.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking the LSAT, enrolling in a structured bar-preparation course, or spending an additional year improving your class standing before reapplying. These steps can directly address the factors that most affected your current outcome. (218 words)
